title: "Mass matrices and posterior geometry"

The [HMC
trajectory](hamiltonian-monte-carlo.qmd#potential-kinetic-and-total-energy)
first transformed the passage-level Student-$t$ posterior so that its two
directions had comparable scales. We call this transformation **whitening**
because it aims to produce coordinates having unit variance and zero
correlation. A [**mass
matrix**](https://mc-stan.org/docs/reference-manual/mcmc.html) supplies HMC
with the corresponding scale and orientation for its momentum without
changing the [posterior target](posterior-distributions.qmd).

The [covariance-matrix
primer](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd#vectors-matrices-and-covariance)
defines matrix--vector multiplication, positive definiteness, and the matrix
inverse, then shows that a covariance matrix records marginal variances on its
diagonal and pairwise covariances off diagonal.
[Correlation](../random-variables-and-distributions/correlation.qmd)
rescales those pairwise associations. A mass matrix can adapt to this joint
scale and orientation without changing the posterior probabilities being
sampled.

We begin with one mass in one dimension, extend it to two separate axis
scales, and then ask why a tilted posterior requires a dense matrix. The
passage-level posterior lets us see the resulting whitening transformation
before we connect it to NUTS adaptation.

## From one mass to a dense matrix {#general-kinetic-energy}

Start with one position $q$ and one momentum $\rho$. Choose a positive scalar
mass $m$ and draw

$$
\rho\sim\mathcal N(0,m).
$$

The kinetic energy and position velocity are

$$
K(\rho)=\frac{\rho^2}{2m},
\qquad
v=\frac{\mathrm dq}{\mathrm dt}=\frac{\rho}{m}.
$$

Because $\operatorname{Var}[\rho]=m$, the velocity variance is

$$
\operatorname{Var}[v]
=\operatorname{Var}\!\left[\frac{\rho}{m}\right]
=\frac{1}{m^2}\operatorname{Var}[\rho]
=\frac{1}{m}.
$$

A larger mass therefore produces a smaller range of typical velocities. The
momentum itself varies on the scale $\sqrt m$, but dividing it by $m$ leaves
velocity on the scale $1/\sqrt m$.

Now suppose the position has two coordinates. We can give them separate
masses with the diagonal matrix

$$
M=
\begin{pmatrix}
m_1&0\\
0&m_2
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The zeros say that the two momentum coordinates have no covariance. The
velocity vector is

$$
\mathbf v=M^{-1}\boldsymbol\rho
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\rho_1/m_1\\
\rho_2/m_2
\end{pmatrix},
$$

so its coordinate variances are $1/m_1$ and $1/m_2$. We may therefore move
at one typical speed along the first axis and another along the second.

But what if the posterior contours form a tilted ellipse? Changing the two
axis speeds can widen or narrow that ellipse, but it cannot remove the tilt.
We need a matrix with off-diagonal entries so that a velocity in one
coordinate may also depend on momentum in the other. Such a matrix is called
**dense**.

For a symmetric positive-definite mass matrix $M$, the scalar formulas become

$$
\boldsymbol\rho\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,M),
\qquad
K(\boldsymbol\rho)
=\frac12\boldsymbol\rho^\mathsf TM^{-1}\boldsymbol\rho,
$$

and

$$
\frac{\mathrm d\mathbf q}{\mathrm dt}
=M^{-1}\boldsymbol\rho.
$$

The [matrix
primer](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd#vectors-matrices-and-covariance)
defines positive definiteness and the inverse used here. The leapfrog position
update follows the same pattern:

$$
\mathbf q_{t+1}
=\mathbf q_t+\epsilon M^{-1}\boldsymbol\rho_{t+\frac12}.
$$

Since $\mathbf v=M^{-1}\boldsymbol\rho$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf v)
&=\operatorname{Cov}(M^{-1}\boldsymbol\rho)\\
&=M^{-1}\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol\rho)(M^{-1})^\mathsf T\\
&=M^{-1}MM^{-1}\\
&=M^{-1}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the inverse mass matrix should roughly match posterior covariance: wider
posterior directions receive wider typical velocities. Here $M$ denotes
momentum covariance and $M^{-1}$ denotes velocity covariance. Software may
report either matrix, so we will keep the convention visible whenever we
interpret an adapted value.

## Geometry of the passage-level Student-t model

We can now examine the posterior grid used on the preceding pages. The left
panel of the figure retains the unequal scales and tilt of
$(\mu,\log\sigma)$. The right panel applies a dense whitening transformation
that both rescales and untilts the grid. If separate axis masses were enough,
the second operation would be unnecessary.

```{r}
#| label: provo-mass-matrix-geometry
library(ggplot2)

provo <- read.csv("data/provo/passage-summaries.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
y <- provo$noun_minus_verb_log_ffd
nu <- 4
prior_scale <- 2 * sd(y)
log_sum_exp <- function(x) { m <- max(x); m + log(sum(exp(x - m))) }
log_target <- function(eta) {
  mu <- eta[1]; sigma <- exp(eta[2])
  sum(dt((y - mu) / sigma, df = nu, log = TRUE) - log(sigma)) +
    dnorm(mu, 0, prior_scale, log = TRUE) +
    log(2) + dnorm(sigma, 0, prior_scale, log = TRUE) + eta[2]
}
mode_fit <- optim(c(median(y), log(mad(y))),
                  function(eta) -log_target(eta), method = "BFGS",
                  hessian = TRUE,
                  control = list(reltol = 1e-12, maxit = 1000L))
local_sd <- sqrt(diag(solve(mode_fit$hessian)))
grid <- expand.grid(
  mu = seq(mode_fit$par[1] - 7 * local_sd[1],
           mode_fit$par[1] + 7 * local_sd[1], length.out = 321L),
  log_sigma = seq(mode_fit$par[2] - 7 * local_sd[2],
                  mode_fit$par[2] + 7 * local_sd[2], length.out = 321L)
)
grid$log_kernel <- apply(grid, 1, log_target)
grid$weight <- exp(grid$log_kernel - log_sum_exp(grid$log_kernel))
grid_values <- as.matrix(grid[, c("mu", "log_sigma")])
grid_mean <- colSums(grid_values * grid$weight)
centered <- sweep(grid_values, 2, grid_mean, "-")
covariance <- crossprod(centered * sqrt(grid$weight))
whitening <- solve(t(chol(covariance)))
white <- t(whitening %*% t(centered))
white_covariance <- crossprod(white * sqrt(grid$weight))

geometry <- rbind(
  data.frame(coordinates = "mu, log_sigma",
             variance_1 = covariance[1, 1],
             variance_2 = covariance[2, 2],
             correlation = cov2cor(covariance)[1, 2]),
  data.frame(coordinates = "posterior-whitened",
             variance_1 = white_covariance[1, 1],
             variance_2 = white_covariance[2, 2],
             correlation = cov2cor(white_covariance)[1, 2])
)
stopifnot(length(y) == 55L, all(eigen(covariance)$values > 0))
geometry
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-whitened-geometry
#| fig-cap: "Posterior grid cells before and after dense whitening. Point darkness represents normalized posterior mass."
display <- rbind(
  data.frame(x = centered[, 1], y = centered[, 2], weight = grid$weight,
             coordinates = "centered passage-level Student-t model coordinates"),
  data.frame(x = white[, 1], y = white[, 2], weight = grid$weight,
             coordinates = "posterior-whitened coordinates")
)
display <- subset(display, weight >= quantile(weight, .80))

ggplot(display, aes(x, y, alpha = weight)) +
  geom_point(color = "#8B1A1A", size = .45) +
  facet_wrap(~coordinates, scales = "free") +
  scale_alpha(range = c(.06, .7), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "First coordinate", y = "Second coordinate") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

A unit matrix would give the two coordinates the same mass. A diagonal matrix
could match their separate widths, but the left panel would remain tilted.
The dense transformation produces the more nearly circular cloud on the
right by mixing the coordinates as well as rescaling them. One constant dense
matrix still cannot remove curvature that changes from one posterior region
to another.

Stan estimates a regularized inverse mass matrix during warmup, then holds it fixed during retained sampling. Adaptation must stop because changing the transition indefinitely could change its stationary distribution. The matrix improves computation; it does not alter the 55 passage summaries or repair the passage-level Student-t model's aggregation limits.

To connect this geometry to the R objects, `covariance` estimates the weighted
covariance of the $(\mu,\log\sigma)$ grid cells. Then
`chol(covariance)` factorizes that ellipse, `whitening` applies the inverse
factor, and `white_covariance` checks whether the transformed coordinates have
approximately unit variances and zero correlation.

## Recap and forward link

1. $M$ is momentum covariance; $M^{-1}$ is velocity covariance in this notation.
2. A diagonal matrix rescales axes, while a dense matrix can also rotate global linear correlation.
3. Whitening improves computational geometry without changing the posterior target.
4. A constant matrix cannot eliminate nonlinear curvature that changes across the target.

The [NUTS page](no-u-turn-sampler.qmd#growing-and-stopping-a-trajectory) turns from trajectory geometry to trajectory length.

## Check your understanding

1. Which matrix is the momentum covariance?
2. Why does the inverse mass matrix determine velocity covariance?
3. What can a dense matrix represent that a diagonal one cannot?
4. Why must adaptation end before retained sampling?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The mass matrix $M$ is the covariance of momentum: $\rho\sim\mathcal N(0,M)$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. Because $v=M^{-1}\rho$, $\operatorname{Cov}(v)=M^{-1}MM^{-1}=M^{-1}$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. A dense matrix can represent global linear correlation and rotate the coordinate system; a diagonal matrix can only rescale axes. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. The retained transition must remain fixed to preserve a single stationary distribution; indefinite adaptation would keep changing the kernel. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
